content:
Six people, including two children, were killed on Thursday morning when a suspected natural gas explosion partly collapsed a five-storey apartment building in the Georgian capital, Tbilisi, according to officials quoted by [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/amp/news/2026/11/19/six-killed-in-suspected-gas-explosion-at-georgia-apartment-building).

The blast struck a residential block on Rustavi Highway in Lower Ponichala, a suburb on the eastern edge of the city, bringing down an entire entrance section of the building and trapping residents beneath tonnes of concrete. Rescue teams worked through the day and into the night, completing the search of the wreckage around midnight.

Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili told reporters at the scene that six bodies had been recovered from the rubble, including that of a seven-year-old child and one other minor. Five people were taken to hospital, one of them in a serious condition. Among the survivors was a three-year-old girl, Taia, who was pulled alive from the debris in one of the few hopeful moments of a grim day. Her mother was among those killed, according to the head of Georgia's Emergency Management Service, Temur Mgebrishvili.

Preliminary information points to a gas heater on the fifth floor of the building. Tamazashvili said early findings suggested the heater had malfunctioned, and that a resident had switched it on during the night, turned it off, and switched it on again in the morning, moments before the explosion. The exact cause remains under investigation, and a criminal case has been opened under Article 240 of Georgia's Criminal Code, which covers violations of safety rules.

The rescue operation itself was fraught with danger. At one point a retaining wall at the front of the damaged building began to tilt forward, forcing rescuers to abandon work from that side and continue from the rear. "While the rescue operation was underway, about half an hour ago, a retaining wall tilted forward, and as a result, rescue work from the front was halted," Tamazashvili said during the operation, according to the Georgian news outlet Civil Georgia.

City officials moved quickly to house the displaced. Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said 28 families, more than 100 people in total, would be temporarily relocated to hotels after structural assessments found two entrances of the building unsafe. The rest of the block was judged fit for habitation, and residents of the unaffected sections were allowed to remain in their homes.

Georgia has declared Sunday, November 22, a national day of mourning for the victims. Flags will fly at half-mast, and public events have been cancelled or postponed.

The disaster has revived questions about gas safety in Georgia's ageing Soviet-era housing stock, where many families rely on individual gas heaters through the cold winter months. Safety campaigners have long warned that old pipework, poorly maintained appliances and a lack of regular inspections leave residents exposed, particularly in the large panel apartment blocks built decades ago on the outskirts of the capital.

Thursday's explosion was one of the deadliest residential gas accidents in Georgia in recent years, and it comes at a moment when the country is already on edge. Georgia's eastern neighbour has been the focus of heightened security attention across the region this week, after Russian missiles and a drone came down on Polish territory during a major attack on Ukraine, an incident covered in our report on [Russia's violation of Polish airspace](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/russia-violates-poland-airspace-missiles-drone-november-20-2026). Estonia, meanwhile, announced it would close its border with Russia for at least six months, as reported in our coverage of [Estonia's border closure](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/estonia-closes-russia-border-six-months-december-1-november-2026).

For the families of Ponichala, however, the wider geopolitics of the region will matter little in the days ahead. Funerals for the six victims are expected to take place over the weekend, and investigators will continue examining the wreckage to establish precisely what failed on the fifth floor. The three-year-old girl pulled from the rubble remains in hospital, and officials have not yet said when she will be discharged.

The Interior Ministry has urged residents across the country to have gas appliances checked by qualified technicians and to report any smell of gas immediately, a reminder that in homes heated by gas, a routine winter morning can turn catastrophic in seconds.
summary: A suspected natural gas explosion tore through a five-storey apartment building in Tbilisi's Ponichala district on Thursday morning, killing six people including two children and leaving more than 100 residents homeless. A three-year-old girl was pulled alive from the rubble, and Georgia has declared a national day of mourning.
title: Six killed, including two children, as suspected gas blast collapses Tbilisi apartment block
